desc:
citations[i] is the number of citations of paper i. The h-index is the largest h such that at least h papers have at least h citations each.

You may hand out up to k extra citations in total. Each extra citation goes to one paper of your choice and adds 1 to it; the same paper may receive several. Return the largest h-index you can reach.

Example: citations = [3, 0, 6, 1, 5] has h-index 3. With k = 4 the answer is 4 (give 1 to the paper with 3 and 3 to the paper with 1, so four papers have at least 4). With k = 3 it stays 3.
hints: Try asking the reverse question: for a fixed target h, what is the cheapest way to get h papers with at least h citations?
The cheapest h papers to lift are the h most cited ones, and the cost is the sum of max(0, h - c) over them. If target h is affordable, is target h - 1 affordable too?
Yes, so the answer is the largest h in [0, n] whose cost is at most k. Sort descending once and binary search h, computing each cost in O(h).
editorial: Fix a target h. Out of all ways to choose h papers, picking the h largest citation counts minimises the total deficit sum(max(0, h - c)), since each deficit is a non-increasing function of c. Extra citations spent on any other paper or beyond the threshold are wasted.

Cost is monotone in h: lowering the target removes (or shrinks) deficits of the same top papers, so if h is affordable then so is h - 1. Binary search the largest affordable h in [0, n]. With the array sorted in descending order, each cost evaluation is O(h), so the total is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log n) for the search. Prefix sums make each evaluation O(log n) if you need more speed.
